Subject: Dedicated sizing guidance for RLW-2489

Kimberly —

Thanks for taking time this week. We're moving RLW-2489 (pilot -> reserved) through procurement and need a pragmatic GPU SKU mix recommendation for Dedicated. Primary workload is a mixed real-time chat API (gen + retrieval) with embeddings for storage and occasional long-context summarization jobs. Current peak qps is ~220 concurrent short chat sessions and 15 long-context batches/hour. Latency SLO for short chats is 120–150ms p50 generation; quality sensitivity is high for med-to-large instruction prompts.

We're particularly interested in cost/loss tradeoffs for H100 vs A100 vs L4, and any operational guardrails (holdback capacity, fallbacks) you recommend so we don't blow past the committed spend during spikes. Can you share a concrete playbook and a first-pass capacity split?

— Aisha

Thanks Aisha — quick reply with high-level guidance and I'll loop in Dev/Rishi for sizing calc and holdback ops details. Attached a short perf summary and our holdback calculator.

High-level recommendation (pilot -> reserved):
- H100: allocate for the high-quality, long-context summarization and the heaviest chat paths where larger context and higher FP8 throughput materially improve latency/quality. H100 = high cost, best perf on 80GB SXM for very large models (multi-GPU context).
- A100: good middle ground for chat workloads that need memory and throughput but are not the absolute largest contexts. Pick 80GB A100s if you expect many medium-length contexts that benefit from native bfloat/FP16 kernels.
- L4: low-cost, high-density option for short-turnaround classification, embeddings, and cheap chat fallbacks. Use a separate L4 pool for stateless/quantized variants and cheap embedding endpoints.

Operational guardrails I suggest:
1) 10% reserved "holdback" pool across all SKUs for unexpected spikes and token-heavy tails — we can size this dynamically with the calculator (attached).
2) Hot/cold pool split: hot (prewarmed H100/A100) for steady throughput and low p50; cold (L4 and quantized A100 instances) for background/low-priority and canary traffic.
3) Fallbacks: route to a quantized L4 or 4-bit A100 variant when latency is non-critical and capacity constrained.
4) Smart routing: cost-based routing that prefers L4 for embeddings and off-peak, A100 during steady-state chat, H100 locked for scheduled long-context jobs or premium routes.

Next steps: Dev will run a first-pass sizing by Monday and propose SKU counts. Would you share a 7-day qps trace and a sample of the long-context job sizes?

Best,
Kimberly Park
Director, Deals — Redwood Inference

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.com>
To: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>, rishi.malhotra@redwood.com
Date: 2026-11-19T09:12:00Z
Subject: INTERNAL: draft sizing split + holdback calc for RLW-2489

Team — I ran the numbers using Aisha's summary (220 concurrent short chats, 15 long jobs/hr, session median length ~300 tokens, long jobs ~10k tokens). Summary below and notes on the holdback/fallback plumbing. Spreadsheet attached.

Draft SKU split (initial reserved commit):
- H100 pool: 6 nodes (reserved) — primary for long-context summarization & premium chat routing. Rationale: the long jobs are memory-heavy (10k tokens), expect KV cache and multi-GPU contexts; H100 avoids memory fragmentation and has best throughput for large sequence lengths.
- A100 pool: 18 nodes (reserved) — main steady-state chat traffic. A100 80GB gives a good balance for p50 targets with batching and KV cache.
- L4 pool: 30 nodes (reserved) — embeddings + quantized fallbacks + burst/cheap chat. L4 offers ~3–4x lower per-node cost for stateless workloads; use it for non-SLA-critical routes and embeddings.

Holdback & capacity rules:
- Keep 10% of the aggregate reserved vGPU count as soft holdback: do not commit to customer routes until CA (canary autoscale) or prewarming completes. This is a cushion for token tail events and aggressive cache misses.
- Emergency burst policy: allow burst to on-demand spot H100s up to 15% of reserved H100s for short windows (requires pre-approval, ops playbook).
- Fallback routing hierarchy: primary model (H100/A100) -> quantized A100 4-bit -> L4 quantized 4-bit stateless model -> reduced-beam or compressed response mode (shorter context). Implement circuit-breakers per route to avoid cascading p99 latency failures.

Estimated cost impact (ballpark):
- Moving 10% traffic to L4 fallback reduces token cost by ~28% while increasing p50 for those requests by ~80–120ms (acceptable for embeddings and non-critical replies).
- H100 vs A100 delta for the long jobs is ~2–2.5x cost per effective token but saves ~30–50% latency for 10k-token runs and avoids multi-node orchestration complexity.

Operational notes for implementation:
- Prewarm KV caches for long jobs: maintain a small pool of pinned H100s for scheduled long runs to avoid cold-model mount.
- Autoscale thresholds should be token-aware (tokens/sec) not just qps; long jobs create sustained token load.
- Telemetry: per-route token burn, p50/p95/p99, and fallbacks used. Tie alerts to fallback rate increasing >5% over baseline.

I'll attach the holdback_calculator_v2.xlsx with per-SKU cost curves and a fallback-routing-diagram.png. Rishi, can you sanity-check the numbers for p50 slos and the cost deltas before I send to Aisha?

Thanks,
Dev
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Aisha — attaching final notes and next actions (I've copied the key points inline). We ran a quick sim with real traces and the proposed split meets p50 targets while keeping a ~9.8% effective holdback after accounting for burst reservations.

Key points (finalized):
- Reserved commit: H100 6 / A100 18 / L4 30 (initial). We'll re-evaluate at 30/90/180 days with telemetry.
- Holdback: 10% soft holdback; plus a 15% short-term H100 burst window (on-demand) with automatic billing alerts and approvals.
- Fallbacks: implement quantized A100 variants and an L4 path; circuit-breakers to automatically throttle or shorten responses when fallback hit rate > 5%.
- Prewarm: schedule pinned H100s for nightly long-batch windows (configurable).
